description: A two-panel composite of engineering stress–strain curves for Nb-containing medium-Mn low-density steels. Both panels share identical axes: engineering stress (MPa) on the y-axis, 0–1200 with gridlines at 300/600/900/1200, and engineering strain (%) on the x-axis, 0–40 with ticks at 10/20/30/40; curves are drawn over a light-cyan background. (a) is labelled "0.02Nb steels" in the top-right corner; (b) is labelled "0.04Nb steels". Each panel carries the same legend — "723 K/3 h" (black), "723 K/6 h" (red) and "723 K/9 h" (blue). In (a), the black 3 h and red 6 h curves yield just above the 900 MPa gridline, harden slowly to a plateau close to the 1200 MPa gridline, and extend to roughly 29% and 28% strain; the blue 9 h curve instead fractures early, near 8% strain. In (b), the blue 9 h curve fractures earliest, near 4% strain; the red 6 h curve attains the highest plateau (approaching the 1200 MPa gridline) but stops near 17% strain; the black 3 h curve yields near 900 MPa, hardens gradually and reaches roughly 29% strain. The figure demonstrates that aging beyond 3 h sharply degrades ductility in both steels, and that 0.04Nb aged 723 K/3 h offers the best strength–ductility balance.

subfigures.description: Engineering stress–strain curves of the 0.02Nb steel aged at 723 K for 3 h (black), 6 h (red) and 9 h (blue); stress 0–1200 MPa vs strain 0–40%. The 3 h and 6 h curves yield just above 900 MPa and plateaux near 1200 MPa at ~29% and ~28% strain, while the 9 h curve fractures near 8% strain.

Engineering stress–strain curves of the 0.04Nb steel aged at 723 K for 3 h (black), 6 h (red) and 9 h (blue); same axes as (a). The 3 h curve yields near 900 MPa, hardens gradually and extends to ~29% strain; the 6 h curve reaches the highest plateau (~1200 MPa) but ends near 17% strain; the 9 h curve fractures near 4% strain.

observations.observation: The group consists of two engineering stress–strain panels, (a) labelled "0.02Nb steels" and (b) labelled "0.04Nb steels", both plotted as engineering stress (MPa, 0–1200) versus engineering strain (%, 0–40).
Both legends contain the entries "723 K/3 h" (black curve), "723 K/6 h" (red curve) and "723 K/9 h" (blue curve).
In panel (a), the 0.02Nb blue 9 h curve fractures at the lowest strain of its panel, near the 10% gridline, whereas the 3 h and 6 h curves extend to roughly the 29% and 28% strain levels.
In panel (b), the 0.04Nb blue 9 h curve fractures at a very low strain, well before the 10% gridline, while the red 6 h curve stops near 17% strain and the black 3 h curve reaches about 29% strain.
The 0.04Nb 723 K/6 h (red) curve in panel (b) shows the highest stress plateau of the whole figure, lying close to the 1200 MPa gridline.
All curves in both panels yield at stresses just above the 900 MPa gridline, with no printed numeric yield-strength label.
No numeric data labels or peak values are printed on either panel; only the axis ticks (0/300/600/900/1200 MPa and 0/10/20/30/40%) are readable.
The caption states that the curves are for the 0.02Nb and 0.04Nb steels aged at 723 K for different periods.
Extended aging at 723 K does not markedly alter the yield strength of Nb-containing steels.
The 0.04Nb steel aged at 723 K for 3 h exhibits the most favourable comprehensive mechanical properties.
The figure shows that increasing aging time from 3 h to 9 h drastically shortens elongation in both steels, i.e. it mainly affects ductility rather than yield stress.
